Tension is the anticipation or conflict that keeps the audience interested.
Tension can be created in a variety of ways including:
uncertainty about what will happen next in the story
disagreements, arguments, rivalries between characters
an internal conflict for a character like a moral dilemma or self-doubt
a character's challenge with society's expectations or norms
jealousy, love or betrayal between characters
a character who can’t get what they want.
Tension adds to the depth of the story and keeps the audience interested in the drama, wondering what will happen next!

Aim for three – five hours of schoolwork per day.

List the subjects or topics you need to work on.
Prioritise based on urgency, difficulty, and upcoming assessments.
Each subject should have a minimum of four hours a week dedicated in your timetable.
Ideally you should be completing a module per subject every two weeks.
Divide your available study time into blocks (for example 30 minutes to one hour).
Assign specific subjects or tasks to each block.
Schedule short breaks between learning sessions to recharge.
Avoid long sessions without breaks.
Set achievable goals for each learning session.
Don’t overload your timetable; allow flexibility.
Set reminders for important deadlines.
Consistency is key. Follow your timetable as best you can.
